Caapucú lies on routes south of Asunción. A visit here can include Casa-Oratorio Cabanas, a historic site where visitors explore documents and Paraguay's colonial past. The museum makes for a meaningful stop on the way to the country's other cultural centres.

The collection includes documents associated with the Spanish governor Bernardo de Velasco. Caapucú offers an introduction to the region's history before visits to the missions and museums of San Ignacio Guazú. This stop in town connects local historical heritage with the broader story of colonial Paraguay.

After the first day on the trail, it feels especially good to set down your backpack and settle in under the shelter at Cabaña de Adán. Humid green forest surrounds the camp, with the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta mountains extending beyond the slopes. The evening is spent over dinner and conversations about the ground covered so far, while several more days of hiking lie ahead on the way to the ancient terraces of the Lost City.

Cabaña de Adán is one of the first overnight stops on the route from the village of Mamey to Ciudad Perdida. Travellers rest here after the initial mountain hike and prepare for the next stretch of the trek. The simple camps along this trail allow hikers to spend the night on the route itself, far from city hotels, and head deeper into the mountain forest each day.

On the Ada Tours trip, the itinerary allows approximately 3 hours for the hike from Mamey to the camp, covering a stated distance of 7.6 km. A stop at a natural swimming pool is planned along the way, and the first night is spent in hammocks. Dinner is included on this day of the tour. Accommodation arrangements and the actual progress of the hike are confirmed before departure in light of the current itinerary, weather and trail conditions.

Cachi lies in the Calchaquí Valley in Salta Province, at an elevation of 2,210 metres. White adobe houses line cobblestone streets, with dry mountain slopes rising behind them. The historic centre has retained its small scale and unhurried pace, making it a pleasure to wander from quiet lanes towards the main square.

Around the square stand the Church of San José and the Pío Pablo Díaz Archaeological Museum. Together, they connect the village's colonial history with the valley's much older past. Cachi also offers a glimpse of everyday culture in northern Argentina, from regional cuisine and local festivals to the traditions of communities living among the mountains and high-altitude vineyards.

Cafayate's greatest pride is its aromatic white wines made from Torrontés grapes, a true symbol of northwestern Argentina. Local wineries welcome visitors for tastings and tours, offering a chance to discover the region's winemaking traditions and sample wines produced at the foot of the Andes.

But wine is only part of Cafayate's appeal. The road to town passes through the famous Quebrada de las Conchas, a gorge where wind and water have shaped extraordinary rock formations. Among the best known are the Amphitheatre, the Obelisk and the Devil's Throat. The red, orange and golden tones of the rock are especially vivid under the bright sun of northern Argentina.

Cafayate itself retains the atmosphere of a welcoming provincial town, with peaceful squares, colonial architecture and small cafés and restaurants serving regional dishes. Vineyards stretch beyond the town, backed by rugged mountains.

Cafayate brings together natural scenery and a journey through the region's food and wine. Here you can take a scenic mountain road in the morning, visit a winery in the afternoon and enjoy local cuisine and a glass of wine in the evening while watching the silhouettes of the Andes.

Cafayate is a place where the rugged beauty of the northern Andes meets the art of winemaking, turning a trip into a vivid combination of nature, culture and flavour.
